CHAPTER 17 - ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION AND ALTERNATING CURRENT

Introduction

Oersted showed in 1820 that an electric current produces a magnetic field. A natural question followed: can a magnetic field produce an electric current? Michael Faraday in England and Joseph Henry in America answered YES, independently, around 1831. Their discovery - ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION - is the principle behind electric generators, transformers, induction motors and almost the whole of modern electrical power technology. In this chapter we develop the laws of induction, apply them to the alternating current (AC) that they naturally produce, and analyse how AC behaves in resistors, inductors, capacitors and the series LCR circuit. Plain ASCII notation is used throughout: Phi for magnetic flux, omega for angular frequency, sqrt() for square root, ^2 for squared, and phi for phase angle.

17.1 MAGNETIC FLUX

Magnetic flux Phi through a surface measures the number of magnetic field lines crossing that surface. For a flat coil of area A placed in a uniform magnetic field B, with the normal to the coil making an angle theta with B,
   Phi = B A cos(theta).
If the coil has N turns, the total flux linkage is N Phi. The SI unit of magnetic flux is the WEBER (Wb); 1 Wb = 1 tesla x 1 metre^2 = 1 T m^2. Flux is maximum (Phi = B A) when the field is perpendicular to the plane of the coil (theta = 0), and zero when the field lies in the plane of the coil (theta = 90 degrees). Flux is a scalar; it can be changed by changing B, by changing A, or by rotating the coil (changing theta). Each of these three ways of changing flux is a way to induce an EMF.

17.2 FARADAY'S LAWS OF ELECTROMAGNETIC INDUCTION

Faraday summarised his experiments (moving a magnet into a coil, switching a nearby current on and off) in two laws.
First law: Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a circuit CHANGES, an EMF is induced in the circuit. The induced EMF lasts only as long as the flux keeps changing.
Second law: The magnitude of the induced EMF is equal to the RATE OF CHANGE of magnetic flux linkage. In symbols, for a coil of N turns,
   EMF = -N dPhi/dt.
The minus sign expresses Lenz's law (Section 17.3). If the flux changes from Phi1 to Phi2 in time t, the average induced EMF has magnitude N (Phi2 - Phi1) / t. If the circuit has resistance R, an induced current I = EMF / R flows.

Worked example: A coil of 200 turns and area 5.0 x 10^-3 m^2 sits with its plane perpendicular to a field that falls uniformly from 0.60 T to 0.10 T in 0.20 s. The flux per turn changes by dPhi = A dB = 5.0 x 10^-3 x (0.60 - 0.10) = 2.5 x 10^-3 Wb. Induced EMF = N dPhi/dt = 200 x 2.5 x 10^-3 / 0.20 = 2.5 V.

17.3 LENZ'S LAW AND CONSERVATION OF ENERGY

Lenz's law states: the direction of the induced current is always such that it OPPOSES the change in flux that produces it. When a north pole is pushed toward a coil, the near face of the coil becomes a north pole to repel the magnet; when the magnet is pulled away, the near face becomes a south pole to attract it and oppose its removal. Lenz's law is a statement of the CONSERVATION OF ENERGY. Because the induced current opposes the motion, we must do work against this opposition to keep the magnet moving; that mechanical work is exactly what appears as electrical energy in the circuit. If the induced current instead AIDED the change, the magnet would accelerate on its own and produce energy from nothing - impossible. The minus sign in EMF = -N dPhi/dt is Lenz's law written into Faraday's law.

17.4 MOTIONAL EMF

Consider a straight conductor of length L moving with speed v perpendicular to a uniform field B, its length also perpendicular to both B and v. Free charges in the rod experience a magnetic force qvB; positive charges pile up at one end, negative at the other, until the electric field they set up balances the magnetic force. The resulting potential difference is the MOTIONAL EMF:
   EMF = B L v.
This can also be derived from Faraday's law: as the rod slides along rails, it sweeps out area at rate L v, so dPhi/dt = B L v. If the rod is part of a circuit of resistance R, the current is I = B L v / R, and the power dissipated, P = (B L v)^2 / R, equals the mechanical power needed to drag the rod against the magnetic braking force F = B I L. Energy is conserved.

Worked example: A rod of length 0.50 m moves at 4.0 m/s perpendicular to a 0.20 T field. EMF = B L v = 0.20 x 0.50 x 4.0 = 0.40 V. If the circuit resistance is 2.0 ohm, I = 0.40 / 2.0 = 0.20 A.

17.5 EDDY CURRENTS

When a solid piece of metal is exposed to a changing magnetic flux, induced currents flow in closed loops within the body of the metal. These circulating currents are called EDDY CURRENTS. By Lenz's law they oppose the change that produces them, so they damp the motion (used in electromagnetic braking, moving-coil galvanometer damping and induction heating). Eddy currents also waste energy as heat in transformer and motor cores; to reduce them the cores are LAMINATED (built from thin insulated sheets) so the induced loops are confined to small cross-sections of high resistance, cutting the eddy-current losses.

17.6 SELF-INDUCTION AND SELF-INDUCTANCE

When the current in a coil changes, the flux it produces through itself changes, and by Faraday's law the coil induces an EMF in ITSELF that opposes the change of current. This is SELF-INDUCTION. The flux linkage is proportional to the current, N Phi = L I, where L is the SELF-INDUCTANCE (or simply inductance) of the coil. The self-induced (back) EMF is
   EMF = -L dI/dt.
The SI unit of inductance is the HENRY (H); a coil has an inductance of 1 H if a current changing at 1 A/s induces an EMF of 1 V. For a long solenoid of n turns per metre, length l and cross-sectional area A, L = mu0 n^2 A l. Inductance depends only on geometry and the core material; a coil wound on an iron core has a much larger L than an air-cored coil. Self-inductance is the electrical analogue of inertia - it opposes CHANGES in current.

17.7 MUTUAL INDUCTION

When two coils are placed near each other, a changing current in the first (primary) coil produces a changing flux through the second (secondary) coil and induces an EMF in it. This is MUTUAL INDUCTION. The flux through the second coil is proportional to the current in the first: N2 Phi2 = M I1, and the EMF induced in the second coil is
   EMF2 = -M dI1/dt,
where M is the MUTUAL INDUCTANCE of the pair, also measured in henry. M depends on the geometry, the number of turns of both coils, their separation and orientation, and the core material. Mutual induction is the operating principle of the transformer.

17.8 ENERGY STORED IN AN INDUCTOR

To build up a current in an inductor, the source must do work against the back EMF. The energy delivered is stored in the magnetic field of the coil. Starting from rest, the work done to raise the current to a final value I is
   U = 1/2 L I^2.
This is analogous to the kinetic energy 1/2 m v^2 of a moving mass (L plays the role of mass, I of velocity). When the current is switched off, this stored energy is returned to the circuit - which is why breaking an inductive circuit can produce a spark.

Worked example: The energy stored in a 0.50 H inductor carrying 3.0 A is U = 1/2 x 0.50 x 3.0^2 = 0.5 x 0.50 x 9.0 = 2.25 J.

17.9 THE AC GENERATOR

An AC generator (alternator) converts mechanical energy into electrical energy using electromagnetic induction. A coil of N turns and area A is rotated with constant angular speed omega in a uniform magnetic field B. The flux linkage at time t is N Phi = N B A cos(omega t), so by Faraday's law the induced EMF is
   EMF = -d(N Phi)/dt = N B A omega sin(omega t) = E0 sin(omega t),
with peak EMF E0 = N B A omega. The output is therefore a sinusoidal ALTERNATING EMF whose polarity reverses every half rotation. This is the origin of the alternating current supplied by the mains.

17.10 ALTERNATING CURRENT AND VOLTAGE

An alternating current varies sinusoidally with time:
   I = I0 sin(omega t),   V = V0 sin(omega t),
where I0 and V0 are the PEAK (maximum) values, omega = 2 pi f is the angular frequency and f is the frequency (50 Hz for the Indian mains). The current reverses direction every half cycle. Because the average of a sinusoid over a full cycle is zero, we describe AC using the ROOT-MEAN-SQUARE (RMS) value.

17.11 RMS AND PEAK VALUES

The RMS value of an alternating current is the steady (DC) current that would produce the SAME heating in a resistor. Averaging I^2 = I0^2 sin^2(omega t) over a cycle gives mean(I^2) = I0^2 / 2, so
   I_rms = I0 / sqrt(2) = 0.707 I0,   and similarly   V_rms = V0 / sqrt(2).
The Indian mains value 220 V is an RMS value; its peak is V0 = 220 x sqrt(2) = 311 V. AC ammeters and voltmeters read RMS values. The average power in a resistor is P = I_rms V_rms = I_rms^2 R.

17.12 AC THROUGH A RESISTOR, INDUCTOR AND CAPACITOR

(a) Pure resistor R: V = V0 sin(omega t) gives I = (V0/R) sin(omega t). Current and voltage are IN PHASE (phase difference 0). Ohm's law holds for RMS values: I_rms = V_rms / R.
(b) Pure inductor L: the current LAGS the voltage by 90 degrees (pi/2). The inductor opposes changes in current, and its opposition is the INDUCTIVE REACTANCE
   X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L,
measured in ohm. X_L increases with frequency, so an inductor blocks high-frequency AC and passes DC (at f = 0, X_L = 0). Then I_rms = V_rms / X_L.
(c) Pure capacitor C: the current LEADS the voltage by 90 degrees. Its opposition is the CAPACITIVE REACTANCE
   X_C = 1 / (omega C) = 1 / (2 pi f C),
measured in ohm. X_C decreases with frequency, so a capacitor passes high-frequency AC and blocks DC (at f = 0, X_C is infinite). Then I_rms = V_rms / X_C.

17.13 THE SERIES LCR CIRCUIT AND IMPEDANCE

When a resistor R, inductor L and capacitor C are connected in series across an AC source, the same current flows through all three, but the voltages across them are out of phase. Adding them as phasors, the total opposition to AC is the IMPEDANCE Z:
   Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2),
and the RMS current is I_rms = V_rms / Z. The current differs in phase from the applied voltage by phi, where
   tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C) / R.
If X_L > X_C the circuit is net inductive (current lags voltage); if X_C > X_L it is net capacitive (current leads). The quantity (X_L - X_C) is the net reactance.

Worked example: In a series circuit R = 30 ohm, X_L = 60 ohm, X_C = 20 ohm. Net reactance = 60 - 20 = 40 ohm. Z = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = sqrt(900 + 1600) = sqrt(2500) = 50 ohm. If V_rms = 100 V, then I_rms = 100/50 = 2.0 A, and tan(phi) = 40/30, so phi = 53 degrees (current lags).

17.14 RESONANCE IN A SERIES LCR CIRCUIT

As the frequency is varied, X_L = omega L rises while X_C = 1/(omega C) falls. At one particular frequency they are equal, X_L = X_C, the net reactance vanishes, and the impedance is a minimum, Z = R. This is RESONANCE. Setting omega L = 1/(omega C) gives the RESONANT ANGULAR FREQUENCY
   omega0 = 1 / sqrt(L C),   and   f0 = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)).
At resonance the current is a maximum (I = V/R), the circuit behaves as if purely resistive (phi = 0, power factor 1), and the voltages across L and C are equal and opposite. Series resonant circuits are used to TUNE radios and TVs to a chosen station frequency.

Worked example: For L = 2.0 H and C = 8.0 microF (8.0 x 10^-6 F), omega0 = 1/sqrt(2.0 x 8.0 x 10^-6) = 1/sqrt(1.6 x 10^-5) = 1/(4.0 x 10^-3) = 250 rad/s. Then f0 = 250/(2 pi) = 39.8 Hz.

17.15 POWER IN AC CIRCUITS AND POWER FACTOR

The instantaneous power in an AC circuit varies with time. Its average over a cycle is
   P = V_rms I_rms cos(phi),
where phi is the phase angle between voltage and current. The factor cos(phi) is called the POWER FACTOR. For a pure resistor phi = 0 and cos(phi) = 1 (all supplied power is consumed). For a pure inductor or pure capacitor phi = 90 degrees and cos(phi) = 0: no net power is consumed over a cycle - such a current is called WATTLESS current, because energy is alternately stored and returned by the reactive element. In terms of the circuit, cos(phi) = R / Z. A low power factor means large currents for a given real power, so power engineers try to keep the power factor near 1.

17.16 THE TRANSFORMER

A transformer changes an alternating voltage from one value to another using mutual induction. It has a PRIMARY coil of Np turns and a SECONDARY coil of Ns turns wound on a common laminated soft-iron core. An alternating voltage Vp applied to the primary sets up a changing flux in the core, which links the secondary and induces a voltage Vs. If the flux linkage per turn is the same for both coils,
   Vs / Vp = Ns / Np,
the TURNS RATIO. If Ns > Np the transformer STEPS UP the voltage; if Ns < Np it STEPS DOWN. For an ideal (loss-free) transformer, input power equals output power, Vp Ip = Vs Is, so the current ratio is the inverse of the voltage ratio: Is / Ip = Np / Ns. A step-up transformer raises voltage but lowers current in the same proportion. Transformers work only on AC (a steady DC gives no changing flux). Real transformers lose a little energy to copper (I^2 R) losses, eddy currents and hysteresis, but well-designed units are over 95 percent efficient. Transformers make long-distance power transmission at high voltage (and hence low current, low I^2 R loss) practical.

Worked example: A transformer with Np = 1000 turns and Ns = 100 turns has 230 V applied to the primary. Vs = Vp x Ns/Np = 230 x 100/1000 = 23 V (a step-down transformer). If the secondary delivers 2.0 A, the ideal primary current is Ip = Vs Is / Vp = 23 x 2.0 / 230 = 0.20 A.

SUMMARY

- Magnetic flux Phi = B A cos(theta); unit weber (Wb). Changing flux induces an EMF (Faraday).
- Faraday's law: EMF = -N dPhi/dt. Lenz's law (the minus sign): induced current opposes the change, a consequence of energy conservation.
- Motional EMF of a rod: EMF = B L v. Eddy currents are induced loops in bulk metal; reduced by laminating cores.
- Self-inductance L: EMF = -L dI/dt; energy stored U = 1/2 L I^2. Mutual inductance M: EMF2 = -M dI1/dt. Unit henry (H).
- AC: I = I0 sin(omega t); I_rms = I0/sqrt(2), V_rms = V0/sqrt(2). Mains 220 V is RMS (peak 311 V).
- Reactances: X_L = omega L (current lags), X_C = 1/(omega C) (current leads). Resistor: in phase.
- Series LCR: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2); tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C)/R. Resonance at omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC), Z = R minimum, current maximum.
- Power P = V_rms I_rms cos(phi); power factor cos(phi) = R/Z. Pure reactance -> wattless current.
- Transformer: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np; ideal Vp Ip = Vs Is. Step-up/step-down; works on AC only; cores laminated to cut eddy losses.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Electromagnetic Induction and Alternating Current
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show your working for numerical problems and state the formula used. Take sqrt(2) = 1.414 and pi = 3.14 where required.

questions.question: Define magnetic flux and state its SI unit. Write the expression for the flux through a flat coil of N turns and area A in a uniform field B whose normal makes angle theta with B.
questions.answer: Magnetic flux Phi through a surface is the total number of magnetic field lines crossing that surface; for a flat coil it is Phi = B A cos(theta). For N turns the flux linkage is N Phi = N B A cos(theta). The SI unit of magnetic flux is the weber (Wb); 1 Wb = 1 T m^2. Flux is maximum (Phi = B A) when theta = 0 (field perpendicular to the coil plane) and zero when theta = 90 degrees.
questions.explanation: Definition, formula Phi = B A cos(theta), and unit weber.

questions.question: State Lenz's law and explain how it is a consequence of the conservation of energy.
questions.answer: Lenz's law: the direction of an induced current is always such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it. If a north pole is pushed toward a coil, the near face becomes a north pole and repels it; if the magnet is withdrawn, the near face becomes a south pole and attracts it. Because the induced current always opposes the motion, an external agent must do work to keep the magnet moving; that mechanical work is converted into the electrical energy of the induced current. If instead the induced current aided the motion, the magnet would speed up on its own and create energy from nothing, violating energy conservation. Hence Lenz's law is required by conservation of energy - and is expressed by the minus sign in EMF = -N dPhi/dt.
questions.explanation: State the law, then argue that an opposing current is the only option consistent with energy conservation.

questions.question: A coil of 500 turns encloses an area of 4.0 x 10^-3 m^2. The magnetic field perpendicular to the coil changes uniformly from 0.30 T to 0.80 T in 0.10 s. Calculate the magnitude of the induced EMF.
questions.answer: Change of flux per turn dPhi = A dB = 4.0 x 10^-3 x (0.80 - 0.30) = 4.0 x 10^-3 x 0.50 = 2.0 x 10^-3 Wb. Induced EMF = N dPhi/dt = 500 x (2.0 x 10^-3) / 0.10 = 500 x 0.020 = 10 V. The magnitude of the induced EMF is 10 V.
questions.explanation: Use EMF = N A dB/dt; worked numerical on Faraday's law.

questions.question: A conducting rod of length 0.80 m moves at 5.0 m/s perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.25 T, with its length perpendicular to both the field and the velocity. Find the motional EMF, and the current if the rod is part of a circuit of resistance 4.0 ohm.
questions.answer: Motional EMF = B L v = 0.25 x 0.80 x 5.0 = 1.0 V. Current I = EMF / R = 1.0 / 4.0 = 0.25 A. (The power dissipated is P = EMF x I = 1.0 x 0.25 = 0.25 W, equal to the mechanical power needed to drag the rod against the magnetic force.)
questions.explanation: Apply EMF = B L v then Ohm's law; worked numerical on motional EMF.

questions.question: Calculate the energy stored in a coil of inductance 0.40 H when it carries a steady current of 5.0 A. What happens to this energy when the circuit is suddenly broken?
questions.answer: Energy stored U = 1/2 L I^2 = 0.5 x 0.40 x (5.0)^2 = 0.5 x 0.40 x 25 = 5.0 J. This energy is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor. When the circuit is suddenly broken, the inductor opposes the rapid fall of current by inducing a large back EMF; the stored 5.0 J is released quickly, often appearing as a spark across the switch contacts.

questions.question: The peak value of an alternating voltage is 311 V and its frequency is 50 Hz. Find its RMS value and its angular frequency omega.

questions.question: A series LCR circuit has R = 30 ohm, an inductor of reactance X_L = 60 ohm and a capacitor of reactance X_C = 20 ohm, connected across a 120 V (RMS) AC supply. (a) Find the impedance Z. (b) Find the RMS current. (c) Find the phase angle phi and state whether the current leads or lags. (d) Find the power factor and the average power consumed.
questions.answer:
(a) Net reactance = X_L - X_C = 60 - 20 = 40 ohm. Impedance Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) = sqrt(30^2 + 40^2) = sqrt(900 + 1600) = sqrt(2500) = 50 ohm.
(b) RMS current I_rms = V_rms / Z = 120 / 50 = 2.4 A.
(c) tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C)/R = 40/30 = 1.333, so phi = 53 degrees. Because X_L > X_C the circuit is net inductive, so the current LAGS the voltage by 53 degrees.
(d) Power factor cos(phi) = R/Z = 30/50 = 0.60. Average power P = V_rms I_rms cos(phi) = 120 x 2.4 x 0.60 = 172.8 W (equivalently I_rms^2 R = 2.4^2 x 30 = 172.8 W).

questions.question: A series LCR circuit contains an inductor L = 2.0 H and a capacitor C = 8.0 microF. (a) Find the resonant angular frequency omega0 and the resonant frequency f0. (b) State what happens to the impedance and current at resonance. (c) Give one practical use of series resonance.
questions.answer:
(a) At resonance X_L = X_C, giving omega0 = 1/sqrt(L C). Here L C = 2.0 x 8.0 x 10^-6 = 1.6 x 10^-5 s^2, so sqrt(L C) = 4.0 x 10^-3 s and omega0 = 1/(4.0 x 10^-3) = 250 rad/s. Then f0 = omega0/(2 pi) = 250/6.28 = 39.8 Hz (about 40 Hz).
(b) At resonance the net reactance (X_L - X_C) is zero, so the impedance is a minimum, Z = R, and the current is a maximum, I = V/R. The circuit behaves as if purely resistive (phase angle 0, power factor 1), and the voltages across L and C are equal and opposite.
(c) Series resonant circuits are used to TUNE radios and televisions: adjusting C (or L) sets the resonant frequency equal to the desired station frequency, so that station's signal produces the largest current while others are suppressed.
questions.explanation: Apply omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC); explain minimum Z, maximum I, and tuning application.

questions.question: A step-down transformer has 2000 turns in its primary and 50 turns in its secondary. The primary is connected to a 240 V AC supply. (a) Find the secondary voltage. (b) If the transformer is ideal and the secondary delivers 8.0 A, find the primary current.
questions.answer:
(a) Vs / Vp = Ns / Np, so Vs = Vp x Ns/Np = 240 x 50/2000 = 240 x 0.025 = 6.0 V. Since Ns < Np this is a step-down transformer.
(b) For an ideal transformer input power equals output power: Vp Ip = Vs Is, so Ip = Vs Is / Vp = 6.0 x 8.0 / 240 = 48/240 = 0.20 A. The primary current (0.20 A) is much smaller than the secondary current (8.0 A) - a step-down transformer lowers voltage but raises current.

questions.question: What are eddy currents? Give one useful application and explain how eddy-current losses are reduced in a transformer core.
questions.answer: Eddy currents are circulating induced currents set up in the body of a solid conductor when the magnetic flux through it changes; by Lenz's law they flow so as to oppose the change. Useful application: electromagnetic (eddy-current) braking, in which currents induced in a moving metal disc oppose its motion and bring it smoothly to rest (also used in induction heating and galvanometer damping). In a transformer, eddy currents flowing in the iron core dissipate energy as heat. To reduce these losses the core is LAMINATED - built from thin sheets of iron insulated from one another - so the induced current loops are confined to thin, high-resistance sections, greatly reducing the eddy currents and the heat they produce.
questions.explanation: Definition, one application, and lamination as the reduction method.

questions.question: A coil of 300 turns and area 2.0 x 10^-3 m^2 has a field perpendicular to it increasing from 0.10 T to 0.40 T in 0.15 s. Find the induced EMF.

questions.answer: The flux Phi = B A cos(theta) can be changed by: (1) changing the magnetic field strength B (e.g. moving a magnet nearer/further, or switching a nearby current); (2) changing the area A of the coil (e.g. a sliding rod on rails); (3) rotating the coil so that the angle theta between the field and the coil's normal changes (as in a generator). Any of these induces an EMF.
questions.explanation: Change B, change A, or change theta.

questions.question: State Lenz's law.
questions.answer: Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is always such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that produces it. In other words, the induced effect acts to keep the flux from changing - repelling an approaching magnet and attracting a receding one.

questions.question: What are eddy currents? Give two applications and one disadvantage.
questions.answer: Eddy currents are circulating induced currents set up in the body of a solid conductor when the flux through it changes; by Lenz's law they oppose the change. Applications: (1) electromagnetic braking (e.g. in trains and moving-coil galvanometers, where they damp motion); (2) induction heating (e.g. induction furnaces and induction cooktops). Disadvantage: they dissipate energy as heat in the iron cores of transformers and motors, lowering efficiency - which is why cores are laminated.

questions.question: A bar magnet is dropped through a vertical copper pipe. Explain why it falls more slowly than through a plastic pipe.
questions.answer: As the magnet falls through the copper pipe, the magnetic flux through each section of the pipe changes, inducing eddy currents in the copper. By Lenz's law these currents flow so as to oppose the change - the section below the magnet repels it and the section above attracts it, both retarding the fall. The magnet therefore experiences an upward magnetic drag and falls slowly (nearly at terminal velocity). A plastic pipe is a non-conductor, so no eddy currents are induced and the magnet falls freely under gravity.
questions.explanation: Eddy currents in copper oppose the motion (Lenz); plastic has none.

questions.question: Derive the expression for the motional EMF of a rod moving in a magnetic field.
questions.answer: Consider a rod of length L moving with speed v perpendicular to a uniform field B, its length perpendicular to both B and v. Each free charge q in the rod experiences a magnetic force F = q v B along the rod. This pushes positive charge to one end and negative to the other, setting up an electric field E inside the rod. Charge separation continues until the electric force q E balances the magnetic force q v B, i.e. E = B v. The potential difference across the rod of length L is EMF = E L = B L v. Equivalently, as the rod sweeps area at the rate L v, dPhi/dt = B L v, giving the same result by Faraday's law.
questions.explanation: Force-balance derivation giving EMF = B L v.

questions.question: A metal rod 1.2 m long moves at 6.0 m/s perpendicular to a field of 0.30 T. Find the induced EMF.
questions.answer: EMF = B L v = 0.30 x 1.2 x 6.0 = 2.16 V. So the induced (motional) EMF is about 2.2 V.

questions.question: Distinguish between self-induction and mutual induction.
questions.answer: Self-induction: when the current in a coil changes, the changing flux it produces through itself induces a back EMF in the SAME coil that opposes the change of current (EMF = -L dI/dt). Mutual induction: when the current in one coil changes, the changing flux links a NEIGHBOURING coil and induces an EMF in that second coil (EMF2 = -M dI1/dt). Self-induction involves a single coil; mutual induction involves two coupled coils.
questions.explanation: One coil vs two coupled coils.

questions.question: Define self-inductance and calculate the energy stored in a 0.60 H coil carrying 4.0 A.
questions.answer: Self-inductance L is the property of a coil by which a change of current in it induces a back EMF; numerically L = flux linkage per unit current (N Phi = L I), and the back EMF is EMF = -L dI/dt. Its unit is the henry. Energy stored: U = 1/2 L I^2 = 0.5 x 0.60 x (4.0)^2 = 0.5 x 0.60 x 16 = 4.8 J.

questions.question: The current in a 0.25 H inductor rises from 0 to 6.0 A in 0.30 s. Find the average back EMF.
questions.answer: Average back EMF = L dI/dt = 0.25 x (6.0 - 0)/0.30 = 0.25 x 20 = 5.0 V.

questions.question: Why is self-inductance called the electrical analogue of inertia?
questions.answer: Mechanical inertia (mass) opposes any change in the velocity of a body. Similarly, self-inductance opposes any change in the current through a coil: when the current tries to increase, the coil induces a back EMF that resists the increase; when it tries to decrease, the back EMF resists the decrease. Because it opposes change of current just as inertia opposes change of motion (and because the stored energy 1/2 L I^2 mirrors the kinetic energy 1/2 m v^2), self-inductance is the electrical analogue of inertia.
questions.explanation: Opposes change of current, like mass opposes change of velocity.

questions.question: Define the RMS value of an alternating current and relate it to the peak value.
questions.answer: The RMS (root-mean-square) value of an alternating current is the value of the steady direct current that would produce the same heating effect in a given resistor over the same time. For a sinusoidal current of peak value I0, averaging I^2 over a cycle gives mean(I^2) = I0^2/2, so I_rms = I0/sqrt(2) = 0.707 I0. Similarly V_rms = V0/sqrt(2).

questions.question: An alternating current has a peak value of 8.0 A. Find (a) its RMS value and (b) the heat produced per second in a 10 ohm resistor.
questions.answer: (a) I_rms = I0/sqrt(2) = 8.0/1.414 = 5.66 A. (b) Power (heat per second) = I_rms^2 R = (5.66)^2 x 10 = 32 x 10 = 320 W. (Using I0^2 R/2 = 64 x 10 / 2 = 320 W confirms this.)
questions.explanation: Apply I_rms = I0/sqrt(2) and P = I_rms^2 R.

questions.question: Describe the working of an AC generator and write the expression for its output EMF.
questions.answer: An AC generator (alternator) has a coil of N turns and area A rotated at constant angular speed omega in a uniform magnetic field B. As the coil rotates, the flux linkage N Phi = N B A cos(omega t) continuously changes. By Faraday's law the induced EMF is EMF = -d(N Phi)/dt = N B A omega sin(omega t) = E0 sin(omega t), with peak EMF E0 = N B A omega. The output is a sinusoidal alternating EMF whose polarity reverses every half rotation - this is the source of mains AC. Mechanical energy (rotating the coil) is converted into electrical energy.
questions.explanation: Rotating coil -> changing flux -> sinusoidal EMF E0 sin(omega t).

questions.question: Define inductive reactance and capacitive reactance and give their formulas.
questions.answer: Inductive reactance X_L is the opposition of an inductor to alternating current: X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L (in ohm); it increases with frequency. Capacitive reactance X_C is the opposition of a capacitor to alternating current: X_C = 1/(omega C) = 1/(2 pi f C) (in ohm); it decreases with frequency. Both are measured in ohm but, unlike resistance, they dissipate no average power.
questions.explanation: X_L = omega L, X_C = 1/(omega C), both in ohm.

questions.question: A 100 ohm resistor, a coil of reactance 160 ohm and a capacitor of reactance 40 ohm are in series across a 200 V RMS supply. Find the impedance and the RMS current.
questions.answer: Net reactance = X_L - X_C = 160 - 40 = 120 ohm. Impedance Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) = sqrt(100^2 + 120^2) = sqrt(10000 + 14400) = sqrt(24400) = 156.2 ohm. RMS current I = V/Z = 200/156.2 = 1.28 A.
questions.explanation: Apply Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2), then I = V/Z.

questions.question: State the phase relationship between current and voltage for a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor in an AC circuit.
questions.answer: Resistor: the current is in phase with the voltage (phase difference 0). Inductor: the current lags the voltage by 90 degrees (pi/2). Capacitor: the current leads the voltage by 90 degrees (pi/2). A useful memory aid is 'CIVIL': in a Capacitor (C) I leads V, while V leads I in an inductor (L).

questions.question: Explain how an inductor and a capacitor behave differently toward direct current and high-frequency AC.
questions.answer: An inductor's reactance X_L = omega L is proportional to frequency. For direct current (f = 0), X_L = 0, so the inductor passes DC freely; for high-frequency AC, X_L is large, so it strongly opposes (blocks) high-frequency AC. A capacitor's reactance X_C = 1/(omega C) is inversely proportional to frequency. For direct current (f = 0), X_C is infinite, so the capacitor blocks DC completely; for high-frequency AC, X_C is small, so it passes high-frequency AC easily. Thus an inductor passes DC but blocks high frequencies, whereas a capacitor blocks DC but passes high frequencies - opposite behaviours.
questions.explanation: X_L rises with f (blocks high f, passes DC); X_C falls with f (passes high f, blocks DC).

questions.question: A series LCR circuit has L = 0.50 H and C = 20 microF. Find its resonant frequency f0.
questions.answer: At resonance omega0 = 1/sqrt(L C). L C = 0.50 x 20 x 10^-6 = 1.0 x 10^-5 s^2, so sqrt(L C) = 3.16 x 10^-3 s and omega0 = 1/(3.16 x 10^-3) = 316 rad/s. The resonant frequency f0 = omega0/(2 pi) = 316/6.28 = 50.3 Hz, about 50 Hz.
questions.explanation: Apply omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC) and f0 = omega0/(2 pi).

questions.question: What is the power factor of an AC circuit? What is its value for a pure resistor and for a pure inductor?
questions.answer: The power factor is the factor cos(phi) in the average power expression P = V_rms I_rms cos(phi), where phi is the phase angle between voltage and current; equivalently cos(phi) = R/Z. For a pure resistor phi = 0, so the power factor cos(phi) = 1 (all supplied power is consumed). For a pure inductor phi = 90 degrees, so the power factor cos(phi) = 0 (no net power is consumed - the current is 'wattless').
questions.explanation: cos(phi) = R/Z; 1 for resistor, 0 for inductor.

questions.question: Explain the principle of a transformer and why it works only on AC.
questions.answer: A transformer works on the principle of mutual induction. It has a primary coil (Np turns) and a secondary coil (Ns turns) wound on a common laminated soft-iron core. An alternating voltage applied to the primary sets up a continuously changing magnetic flux in the core; this changing flux links the secondary and, by Faraday's law, induces an alternating EMF in it, with Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. It works only on AC because a steady DC current produces a constant flux, and a constant flux induces no EMF (Faraday's law needs a CHANGING flux). Hence a transformer cannot change a steady DC voltage.
questions.explanation: Mutual induction; needs changing flux, so AC only.

questions.question: State and explain Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction. A coil of 250 turns and area 8.0 x 10^-3 m^2 is placed perpendicular to a field that changes from 0.20 T to 0.60 T in 0.40 s. Calculate the induced EMF.
questions.answer:
Faraday's laws: (First law) Whenever the magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes, an EMF is induced in it; the EMF exists only while the flux is changing. (Second law) The magnitude of the induced EMF equals the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage, EMF = -N dPhi/dt, N being the number of turns. The minus sign (Lenz's law) shows the induced EMF opposes the change of flux.
Calculation: The flux per turn is Phi = B A (field perpendicular to the coil, cos 0 = 1). Change of flux per turn dPhi = A dB = 8.0 x 10^-3 x (0.60 - 0.20) = 8.0 x 10^-3 x 0.40 = 3.2 x 10^-3 Wb. Induced EMF = N dPhi/dt = 250 x 3.2 x 10^-3 / 0.40 = 250 x 8.0 x 10^-3 = 2.0 V.
questions.explanation: Statement of both laws + worked EMF calculation.

questions.question: State Lenz's law and show, with the example of a magnet approaching a coil, that it is a consequence of the conservation of energy.
questions.answer:
Lenz's law: the induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change in flux producing it. Example: push the north pole of a magnet toward a coil. The flux through the coil increases, so an induced current flows in the coil in the direction that makes the near face a NORTH pole. This north face repels the incoming magnet. To keep pushing the magnet in, an external agent must do WORK against this repulsion. That mechanical work is exactly converted into the electrical energy dissipated by the induced current (as heat in the coil's resistance). Energy is conserved: work in = electrical energy out.
Suppose instead the induced current opposed Lenz's law and made the near face a SOUTH pole. It would then ATTRACT the magnet, pulling it in faster, which would increase the flux and the current still further, attracting it even more - the magnet would accelerate on its own and generate electrical energy without any work being done. This perpetual increase of energy from nothing is impossible. Hence the induced current MUST oppose the change, exactly as Lenz's law requires, in order to conserve energy.
questions.explanation: State law + energy-conservation argument via approaching magnet.

questions.question: A conducting rod PQ of length 0.50 m slides on frictionless horizontal rails at 8.0 m/s in a vertical magnetic field of 0.40 T. The rails are connected by a resistor of 2.0 ohm (rod and rails have negligible resistance). Find (a) the motional EMF, (b) the current, (c) the force needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed, and (d) the power delivered, and verify energy conservation.
questions.answer:
(a) Motional EMF = B L v = 0.40 x 0.50 x 8.0 = 1.6 V.
(b) Current I = EMF/R = 1.6/2.0 = 0.80 A.
(c) The current-carrying rod in the field experiences a magnetic (retarding) force F = B I L = 0.40 x 0.80 x 0.50 = 0.16 N. To move at CONSTANT speed the applied force must balance this, so the force needed = 0.16 N.
(d) Mechanical power delivered by the applied force = F v = 0.16 x 8.0 = 1.28 W. Electrical power dissipated in the resistor = I^2 R = (0.80)^2 x 2.0 = 0.64 x 2.0 = 1.28 W (equivalently EMF x I = 1.6 x 0.80 = 1.28 W). The two are equal, so all the mechanical work done against the magnetic force reappears as electrical energy - energy is conserved.
questions.explanation: Full motional-EMF problem with energy-conservation check.

questions.question: Define self-inductance and derive the expression for the energy stored in an inductor. Hence find the energy stored in a 0.80 H coil carrying 2.5 A, and the energy in a 5.0 mH coil carrying 10 A.
questions.answer:
Self-inductance L of a coil is defined by the flux linkage per unit current, N Phi = L I; equivalently, the back EMF is EMF = -L dI/dt. Its unit is the henry.
Derivation of stored energy: while the current is being built up, at the instant the current is i and rising at rate di/dt, the source must supply a power to overcome the back EMF: P = (L di/dt) x i. The work done in time dt is dW = L i di. Integrating from i = 0 to the final current I: U = integral of L i di from 0 to I = L [i^2/2] from 0 to I = 1/2 L I^2. This energy is stored in the magnetic field of the inductor.
Numericals: (i) U = 1/2 x 0.80 x (2.5)^2 = 0.5 x 0.80 x 6.25 = 2.5 J. (ii) U = 1/2 x 5.0 x 10^-3 x (10)^2 = 0.5 x 5.0 x 10^-3 x 100 = 0.25 J.
questions.explanation: Definition + integration derivation of U = 1/2 L I^2 + two numericals.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by the RMS value of an alternating current and derive its relation to the peak value. If a sinusoidal voltage has RMS value 220 V, find its peak value and its instantaneous value at the instant omega t = 30 degrees.
questions.answer:
The RMS value of an alternating current is the value of the equivalent steady direct current that would dissipate the same heat in a given resistor in the same time. For I = I0 sin(omega t), the instantaneous heating rate is I^2 R = I0^2 sin^2(omega t) R. Over one full cycle the average of sin^2(omega t) is 1/2, so the average of I^2 is I0^2/2. The RMS current is the square root of this mean square: I_rms = sqrt(I0^2/2) = I0/sqrt(2) = 0.707 I0. Similarly V_rms = V0/sqrt(2).
With V_rms = 220 V: peak V0 = V_rms x sqrt(2) = 220 x 1.414 = 311 V. Instantaneous value at omega t = 30 degrees: V = V0 sin(30) = 311 x 0.5 = 155.5 V, about 156 V.
questions.explanation: Definition + mean-square derivation + peak and instantaneous values.

questions.question: A series LCR circuit consists of R = 40 ohm, L = 0.10 H and C = 25 microF connected across a 200 V, 100/(pi) Hz supply (so that omega = 200 rad/s). Find (a) X_L, (b) X_C, (c) the impedance Z, (d) the RMS current, and (e) the phase angle.
questions.answer:
Given omega = 200 rad/s.
(a) X_L = omega L = 200 x 0.10 = 20 ohm.
(b) X_C = 1/(omega C) = 1/(200 x 25 x 10^-6) = 1/(5.0 x 10^-3) = 200 ohm.
(c) Net reactance = X_L - X_C = 20 - 200 = -180 ohm. Impedance Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) = sqrt(40^2 + (-180)^2) = sqrt(1600 + 32400) = sqrt(34000) = 184.4 ohm.
(d) RMS current I = V/Z = 200/184.4 = 1.08 A.
(e) tan(phi) = (X_L - X_C)/R = -180/40 = -4.5, so phi = -77.5 degrees. The negative sign (X_C > X_L) means the circuit is net capacitive and the current LEADS the voltage by about 77.5 degrees.

questions.question: Explain, with reference to how X_L and X_C vary with frequency, why a series LCR circuit has a resonant frequency, and describe what happens to the impedance, current and phase at resonance.
questions.answer:
In a series LCR circuit the inductive reactance X_L = omega L increases with frequency, while the capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(omega C) decreases with frequency. At low frequencies X_C dominates (circuit is net capacitive, current leads); at high frequencies X_L dominates (circuit is net inductive, current lags). Since one rises and the other falls, there is exactly one frequency at which they are EQUAL, X_L = X_C. At that frequency the net reactance (X_L - X_C) is zero.
This is resonance, occurring at omega0 = 1/sqrt(L C). At resonance: (i) the impedance Z = sqrt(R^2 + 0) = R is a MINIMUM; (ii) the current I = V/Z = V/R is a MAXIMUM; (iii) the phase angle phi = 0 (since tan(phi) = 0), so the current is in phase with the voltage and the circuit behaves as if purely resistive, with power factor 1. The equal and opposite voltages across L and C cancel. This sharp maximum in current at omega0 is exploited to tune radios and televisions to a chosen station.
questions.explanation: Opposite frequency dependence forces a crossover; describe minimum Z, maximum I, zero phase.

questions.question: Explain the construction and working of a transformer, state the turns-ratio relation, and solve: an ideal step-up transformer raises 240 V to 2400 V; if the primary has 400 turns and draws 5.0 A, find the number of secondary turns and the secondary current.
questions.answer:
Construction: a transformer has two coils - a primary of Np turns and a secondary of Ns turns - wound on a common laminated soft-iron core. Working: an alternating voltage applied to the primary produces a changing magnetic flux in the core; this changing flux links the secondary and induces an alternating EMF in it (mutual induction). If the flux per turn is common to both coils, Vs/Vp = Ns/Np (the turns ratio). If Ns > Np the voltage is stepped up; if Ns < Np it is stepped down. For an ideal transformer, input power = output power: Vp Ip = Vs Is, so Is/Ip = Np/Ns.
Solution: Ns = Np x Vs/Vp = 400 x 2400/240 = 400 x 10 = 4000 turns. Secondary current Is = Ip x Vp/Vs = 5.0 x 240/2400 = 5.0 x 0.10 = 0.50 A. (As expected, stepping voltage up by 10 steps current down by 10.)

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A rectangular coil of 200 turns and area 5.0 x 10^-2 m^2 is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The field is steadily reduced from 0.80 T to 0.30 T in a time of 0.25 s.

(i) Write the formula for the flux through one turn of the coil.
(ii) Calculate the change in flux per turn.
(iii) Calculate the magnitude of the induced EMF.
(iv) State one factor that would increase the induced EMF.
questions.answer:
(i) Phi = B A cos(theta); here theta = 0 (field perpendicular to the plane), so Phi = B A.
(ii) dPhi = A dB = 5.0 x 10^-2 x (0.80 - 0.30) = 5.0 x 10^-2 x 0.50 = 2.5 x 10^-2 Wb.
(iii) EMF = N dPhi/dt = 200 x (2.5 x 10^-2)/0.25 = 200 x 0.10 = 20 V.
(iv) Any one of: increasing the number of turns N, increasing the area A, using a larger change of field dB, or reducing the time dt (a faster change of flux).
questions.explanation: Faraday's law applied step by step to a shrinking field.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A circular coil is connected to a sensitive galvanometer. A student moves the north pole of a bar magnet toward the coil, then holds it still inside the coil, then withdraws it.

(i) In which of the three stages is there a deflection in the galvanometer?
(ii) During approach, what magnetic polarity does the near face of the coil acquire?
(iii) State the law that decides this polarity.
(iv) Explain how energy is conserved in this process.
questions.answer:
(i) There is a deflection only while the magnet is MOVING - i.e. during the approach and during the withdrawal. While the magnet is held still inside the coil, the flux is constant, so there is no induced EMF and no deflection.
(ii) During approach the flux is increasing, so the near face becomes a NORTH pole (to repel the incoming north pole).
(iii) Lenz's law - the induced current opposes the change producing it.
(iv) The student must do work to push the magnet in against the repulsion (and to pull it out against the attraction). This mechanical work is converted into the electrical energy of the induced current (dissipated as heat in the circuit), so energy is conserved.
questions.explanation: Faraday + Lenz applied to the classic magnet-and-coil demonstration.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A metal rod of length 0.60 m rests on two horizontal rails 0.60 m apart, in a vertical magnetic field of 0.50 T. The rails are joined by a 3.0 ohm resistor. The rod is pushed at a constant 4.0 m/s.

(i) Calculate the motional EMF.
(ii) Calculate the current in the circuit.
(iii) Calculate the force opposing the rod's motion.
(iv) Calculate the power dissipated in the resistor.
questions.answer:
(i) Motional EMF = B L v = 0.50 x 0.60 x 4.0 = 1.2 V.
(ii) Current I = EMF/R = 1.2/3.0 = 0.40 A.
(iii) Opposing force F = B I L = 0.50 x 0.40 x 0.60 = 0.12 N.
(iv) Power dissipated P = I^2 R = (0.40)^2 x 3.0 = 0.16 x 3.0 = 0.48 W (equal to F v = 0.12 x 4.0 = 0.48 W, confirming energy conservation).
questions.explanation: Motional EMF, current, braking force and power.

(i) Calculate the average back EMF induced in the coil.
(ii) Calculate the energy stored when the current is 6.0 A.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The voltage supplied to a home is described as 230 V, 50 Hz AC. A resistive heater of 46 ohm is connected to it.

(i) Is 230 V a peak or an RMS value?
(ii) Calculate the peak voltage.
(iii) Calculate the RMS current in the heater.
(iv) Calculate the average power consumed by the heater.
questions.answer:
(i) The quoted mains value 230 V is an RMS value (AC meters read RMS).
(ii) Peak V0 = V_rms x sqrt(2) = 230 x 1.414 = 325 V.
(iii) RMS current I_rms = V_rms/R = 230/46 = 5.0 A.
(iv) Average power P = V_rms I_rms = 230 x 5.0 = 1150 W (equivalently V_rms^2/R = 230^2/46 = 1150 W). For a pure resistor the power factor is 1.
questions.explanation: RMS vs peak and power in a resistive load.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A series circuit contains a resistor R = 60 ohm, an inductor of reactance X_L = 100 ohm and a capacitor of reactance X_C = 20 ohm, connected to a 200 V RMS source.

(i) Calculate the net reactance.
(ii) Calculate the impedance Z.
(iii) Calculate the RMS current.
(iv) Does the current lead or lag the voltage? Justify.
questions.answer:
(i) Net reactance = X_L - X_C = 100 - 20 = 80 ohm.
(ii) Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2) = sqrt(60^2 + 80^2) = sqrt(3600 + 6400) = sqrt(10000) = 100 ohm.
(iii) I = V/Z = 200/100 = 2.0 A.
(iv) Since X_L > X_C the circuit is net inductive, so the current LAGS the voltage. The phase angle is tan(phi) = 80/60 = 1.33, phi = 53 degrees (lagging).
questions.explanation: Series LCR impedance, current and phase interpretation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In an experiment the frequency of the AC source applied to a fixed series LCR circuit is slowly increased from a very low value to a very high value.

(i) How does X_L change as the frequency rises?
(ii) How does X_C change as the frequency rises?
(iii) At low frequency, is the circuit net inductive or net capacitive?
(iv) What special condition occurs at the frequency where X_L = X_C, and how does the current behave there?
questions.answer:
(i) X_L = omega L increases as the frequency rises.
(ii) X_C = 1/(omega C) decreases as the frequency rises.
(iii) At low frequency X_C is large and X_L is small, so X_C > X_L: the circuit is net CAPACITIVE (current leads the voltage).
(iv) When X_L = X_C the net reactance is zero - this is RESONANCE, at omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC). There the impedance is a minimum (Z = R) and the current reaches its MAXIMUM value V/R, in phase with the voltage.
questions.explanation: Frequency dependence of reactances leading to resonance.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A series LCR circuit used to tune a radio has L = 0.20 mH and a variable capacitor. The resistance is small.

(i) Write the formula for the resonant frequency.
(ii) Calculate the capacitance needed for resonance at an angular frequency of 1.0 x 10^6 rad/s.
(iii) What is special about the impedance at resonance?
(iv) Why is a low resistance desirable for good tuning?
questions.answer:
(i) omega0 = 1/sqrt(L C), so C = 1/(omega0^2 L).
(ii) C = 1/(omega0^2 L) = 1/((1.0 x 10^6)^2 x 0.20 x 10^-3) = 1/(1.0 x 10^12 x 2.0 x 10^-4) = 1/(2.0 x 10^8) = 5.0 x 10^-9 F = 5.0 nF.
(iii) At resonance the impedance is a minimum and equals R (the net reactance is zero), so the current is a maximum.
(iv) A low resistance makes the resonance peak sharp (high selectivity), so the circuit responds strongly to the chosen station frequency and only weakly to nearby frequencies, giving clear tuning.
questions.explanation: Resonance condition used for radio tuning; solve for C.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Electric power is generated at 11 kV and transmitted over long distances. A step-up transformer raises it to 220 kV for the transmission line; near towns a step-down transformer lowers it again.

(i) Write the transformer turns-ratio relation.
(ii) For the step-up transformer, is Ns greater or smaller than Np?
(iii) An ideal step-up transformer takes 11 kV, 2000 A and outputs 220 kV. Find the output current.
(iv) Why is power transmitted at high voltage?
questions.answer:
(i) Vs/Vp = Ns/Np (and for an ideal transformer Vp Ip = Vs Is).
(ii) For a step-up transformer Vs > Vp, so Ns is GREATER than Np.
(iii) Ideal transformer: Vp Ip = Vs Is, so Is = Vp Ip/Vs = (11 x 10^3 x 2000)/(220 x 10^3) = (2.2 x 10^7)/(2.2 x 10^5) = 100 A.
(iv) At high voltage the current is smaller (for the same power), so the I^2 R heating losses in the transmission cables are much smaller, making long-distance transmission efficient.
questions.explanation: Transformer turns ratio and the reason for high-voltage transmission.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The iron core of a transformer is not a solid block but is made of many thin sheets of iron, each coated with an insulating varnish and stacked together.

(i) What are the currents that this design is meant to reduce?
(ii) Why do these currents arise in the core?
(iii) How does lamination reduce them?
(iv) State one other place where such currents are deliberately used.
questions.answer:
(i) The design is meant to reduce EDDY CURRENTS in the core.
(ii) The alternating current in the windings produces a changing magnetic flux in the core; by Faraday's and Lenz's laws this changing flux induces circulating (eddy) currents in the conducting iron.
(iii) Lamination breaks the core into thin insulated sheets, so the induced current loops are confined to thin sections of high electrical resistance. This greatly reduces the eddy currents and the heat (I^2 R loss) they produce.
(iv) Eddy currents are deliberately used in electromagnetic braking (e.g. trains, moving-coil galvanometer damping) and in induction heating (induction furnaces, induction cooktops).
questions.explanation: Eddy currents, their origin, and reduction by lamination.
